authors: McCombs, J.W., Herold, N.D., Burkhalter, S.G. & Robinson, C.J.
title: Accuracy assessment of NOAA Coastal Change Analysis Program 2006-2010 land cover and land cover change data
relevance: The published accuracy assessment of one of our two references: national overall accuracy 84.0% (kappa 0.83), Oregon/Washington region 84.9%, with a 3x3-pixel sample unit and a six-of-nine homogeneity rule, meaning C-CAP was never validated at the single-pixel scale we are comparing against. It also states outright that C-CAP is intended for county-to-national use and should be treated only as a screening tool for local or site-specific decisions - so some of our 15-17% disagreement is C-CAP being used outside its validated scale, not model error. Notably, interpreters were allowed a 'fuzzy' alternate call when no single dominant class could be identified, which is a working answer to our 'unsure' response question: record an alternate rather than exclude.

title: Thematic accuracy assessment of the NLCD 2019 land cover for the conterminous United States
relevance: Reports Level II overall accuracy of 77.5% +/- 1% against the primary reference label alone, rising to 87.1% +/- 0.7% when either the primary or an alternate label counts as agreement - a ten-point swing produced purely by how interpreter uncertainty is scored. That is the single most important number for us: it shows that reference ambiguity, handled two defensible ways, moves accuracy by more than our entire model-quality range, which is consistent with finding 2 (IoU 0.49-0.76 not moving recall). Adopt the primary/alternate scheme in our 250-point protocol and report both numbers.

title: Assessing the accuracy of land cover change with imperfect ground reference data
relevance: Quantifies how reference error distorts accuracy: a 10% reference error under-estimated producer's accuracy by 18.5% when errors were independent but over-estimated it by 12.3% when errors were correlated - so the direction of the bias depends on whether reference and map errors share a cause. This is decisive for finding 4: our labels and our references both come from imagery interpretation of the same scenes, so errors are almost certainly correlated and our recall numbers are likely optimistic, not pessimistic. It also introduces the latent-class route to estimating accuracy without a gold standard, which is the only principled way out of finding 5's 'we cannot tell whether it became more correct'.

title: Global and local assessment of image classification quality on an overall and per-class basis without ground reference data
relevance: Shows how to estimate a full confusion matrix and per-class accuracy for several classifications using only their mutual agreement pattern, with no ground reference at all, via latent class modeling. This is the direct method for our situation: treat C-CAP, the NDVI+CHM reference, and the model as three imperfect tests of the same latent canopy variable and solve for each one's sensitivity and specificity. It converts the 15-17% disagreement from an unresolvable annoyance into the actual signal the estimator uses, and would let us say which reference is more liberal in error terms rather than just in area terms.

title: Mapping forest cover and change as continuous variables is essential to advance consistency across forest monitoring products
relevance: Argues that most cross-product forest disagreement is manufactured by thresholding a continuous canopy variable at different cut points, and that reporting continuous cover removes disagreement that is definitional rather than empirical. Applies directly: our NDVI reference and C-CAP are two different thresholds on the same underlying vegetation continuum, which explains why one is systematically more liberal and why the disagreement is spatially concentrated in intermediate-cover pixels. Suggests reporting per-crown canopy as a continuous fraction with the threshold stated, rather than a binary mask, so future comparisons are not hostage to our cut point.

title: Representation of tree cover in global land cover products: Finland as a case study area
relevance: Head-to-head comparison of how several land cover products represent tree cover over the same ground, attributing differences to class definitions, minimum mapping unit, and the treatment of sparse and short canopy. Gives us published disagreement magnitudes to benchmark our 15-17% against, and shows this level of inter-product disagreement is normal rather than a symptom of something broken in our pipeline. Supports treating reference disagreement as an error-budget term to be reported, not a defect to be eliminated.
